frying_pan.hint: A wok is even better here — keep it screaming hot and toss instead of stirring.

gas_stove.hint: Induction works; heat the pan dry for a full minute first so the rice sears instead of sweating.

steps: Day-old rice is the whole game. Spread 2 cups on a plate and break the clumps apart with wet hands — freshly cooked rice steams instead of frying.
Beat 2 eggs with a pinch of salt. Slice 2 scallions, keeping the whites and greens apart.
Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wide pan over high heat until it shimmers. Add the eggs, scramble 20 seconds, and pull them out while still glossy.

Add another tbsp of oil and the scallion whites, fry 15 seconds, then add the rice. Press it flat against the pan for 30 seconds before stirring — that dry contact is what makes it taste fried rather than steamed.
Return the eggs, season with 1/2 tsp salt and a splash of light soy sauce, toss 30 seconds, and finish with the scallion greens.

wok.hint: No wok? Use a large skillet over the highest heat your stove gives — work in two batches so the chicken sears instead of steaming.

dried_chili.hint: No dried chilies? Swap in 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes with a pinch of black pepper.

steps: Cut the chicken into 3/4-inch cubes. Toss with 1 tsp cornstarch and 1 tsp light soy sauce, then rest for 10 minutes.
Mix the sauce in a small bowl: 1 tbsp light soy sauce, 1 tsp dark soy sauce (optional), 1 tbsp Chinkiang vinegar, 1 tsp sugar, 1 tsp cornstarch.
Heat 1 tbsp oil until it shimmers. Add the chicken in a single layer and let it sit untouched for 90 seconds before stirring.
Push the chicken to one side, add garlic and dried chilies to the oil, and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the sauce and stir for 1 minute until it thickens and coats the chicken. Finish with scallion. Serve hot with rice.

frying_pan.hint: A wok works too — just keep the heat slightly lower so the eggs don't catch.

gas_stove.hint: An induction cooktop works fine; give the pan an extra minute to come up to temperature.

steps: Beat 3 eggs with a pinch of salt. Cut 2 tomatoes into wedges.
Heat 1 tbsp oil over medium-high. Pour in the eggs and wait 10 seconds, then fold gently until just set. Remove and set aside.
Add the tomatoes to the dry pan. Cook 3–4 minutes until they collapse and release their juice.
Add 1/2 tsp sugar (this is what balances the acidity — don't skip it) and 1/4 tsp salt.
Return the eggs, fold once or twice to combine, and serve immediately over rice.

wok.hint: A deep skillet works; stir more gently so the tofu cubes stay whole.

minced_pork.hint: No pork? Finely chop beef sirloin, or skip the meat entirely for a vegetarian version.

steps: Cut the tofu into 3/4-inch cubes and soak in hot salted water for 5 minutes. Drain well — this stops it breaking apart.
Brown the minced pork in 1 tbsp oil over high heat until the fat renders, about 2 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp doubanjiang and minced garlic. Fry 30 seconds until the oil turns red.
Add 3/4 cup water, bring to a simmer, and slide in the tofu. Simmer gently for 4 minutes.
Thicken with a cornstarch slurry (1 tsp cornstarch + 2 tsp water), stir once, and finish with ground Sichuan peppercorn and scallion.

frying_pan.hint: No skillet? Blanch in a pot and finish with a garlic-oil drizzle.

gas_stove.hint: An electric hob works; expect an extra minute to get things sizzling.

steps: Cut the broccoli into even florets and soak 5 minutes in cold water, then drain very well.
Heat 1 tbsp oil over medium-high, add sliced garlic, and fry for 20 seconds until fragrant but not brown.
Add the broccoli and stir-fry 2 minutes without water — the wok-dry heat is the point.
Splash in 2 tbsp water, cover for 90 seconds to steam the stems, then uncover and finish on high heat.
Season with salt and an optional drizzle of oyster sauce.

steamer_pot.hint: No steamer? Set a steaming rack inside a deep pot with 1 inch of simmering water, cover with a lid, and steam in a heatproof bowl.

steps: Beat 3 eggs with 1 1/2 cups warm water (not hot) and 1/2 tsp salt — the ratio is 1 part egg to 1.5 parts water.
Strain the mixture through a sieve into a shallow bowl and skim off the bubbles. This is the whole secret to a smooth custard.
Cover the bowl with a plate or foil. Steam over gently simmering water for 10 minutes — never a rolling boil.
Rest 2 minutes, then drizzle with light soy sauce and sesame oil. Serve warm.

clay_pot.hint: No clay pot? A heavy-bottomed stockpot with the lid on gives nearly the same result — just check the liquid every 20 minutes.

steps: Cut pork belly into 1-inch cubes. Blanch in boiling water for 3 minutes, then rinse and pat dry.
Caramelize 2 tbsp sugar in 1 tbsp oil over medium heat until amber, then add the pork and coat evenly.
Add ginger, star anise, 2 tbsp Shaoxing wine, 1 tbsp dark soy sauce, and hot water to cover.
Simmer covered for 60 minutes over the lowest heat until a chopstick slides through cleanly.
Uncover and reduce on high heat for 10 minutes until the sauce clings to each cube and turns glossy.
